drills.q: Define all five of Meszaros's test doubles with one distinguishing sentence each.
drills.a: Dummy: passed but never used (fills a required parameter). Stub: returns canned data, never itself asserted on. Spy: records calls, asserted on after the fact. Mock: pre-programmed expectations that make the double itself fail the test on violation. Fake: a real, lightweight, working implementation (e.g. in-memory repository).

drills.q: Explain the classicist vs mockist testing schools and state which one produces tests that survive refactors better, with a reason.
drills.a: Classicist (Beck/Fowler) prefers real collaborators or fakes and asserts on state/outcomes; mockist (Freeman/Pryce) verifies the interaction/conversation between objects. Classicist-style tests survive refactors better because they assert WHAT happened (observable outcome) rather than HOW it happened (exact call sequence), so internal reordering that preserves behavior doesn't break them.

drills.q: A test suite has tests that pass individually but fail when run in a specific different order. Diagnose the root cause and the fix.
drills.a: A fixture scoped broader than test lifetime (module- or session-scoped) is returning a mutable object that a prior test mutated -- a real, deterministic bug, not randomness. Fix: narrow the fixture scope to function-level, or explicitly reset/reconstruct state between tests if broader scope is kept for performance reasons.

drills.q: Explain property-based testing's shrinking mechanism and why it matters for debugging compared to a hand-written failing example.
drills.a: On finding a counterexample among hundreds of generated inputs, the framework (Hypothesis, QuickCheck) automatically reduces it toward the smallest input that still violates the stated invariant. This means you debug against a near-minimal repro immediately, skipping the manual reduction step that a large, real-world failing example from a hand-written test usually requires.

drills.q: A new unit test requires 15 lines of mock setup to make a 2-line assertion. What should you actually do, and why is 'just write the setup' the wrong instinct?
drills.a: Treat the disproportionate setup as a design smell: the unit under test likely has too many collaborators. Consider decomposing the class/function so the tested behavior depends on fewer things to fake, rather than normalizing heavy setup -- every future test in that unit will re-pay the same cost otherwise.

drills.q: Write (or describe) a property-based test for a sort function that would catch more bugs than three hand-picked examples, and explain the mechanical reason why.
drills.a: Assert invariants for @given(st.lists(st.integers())): (1) length is preserved, (2) the result is a permutation of the input (sorted(result) == sorted(lst)), (3) it is non-decreasing (result[i] <= result[i+1] for all i), (4) sorting twice equals sorting once (idempotence). This catches bugs on adversarial generated inputs (empty lists, all-duplicates, negative numbers, long lists) that hand-picked examples routinely omit because the test author didn't think to try them.

drills.q: When is property-based testing a poor fit, and what should be used instead? Give a concrete example.
drills.a: Poor fit for logic with no clean general invariant -- e.g., 'if the user's plan is Enterprise and it's a Tuesday, apply an 8% discount' has no elegant mathematical property, just a specific rule. Parametrized example-based tests enumerating the actual business rule cases are correct there instead.

drills.q: How do you unit test a function whose behavior depends on the current time or a random number generator, without making the test itself non-deterministic?
drills.a: Inject the clock/RNG as a dependency rather than calling datetime.now()/random() directly inside the function, then supply a fixed fake clock or seeded/fake RNG in the test. This is one of the few cases where using a stub for a genuinely non-deterministic external boundary is correct even under a classicist philosophy.

drills.q: A property-based test shrinks to a failing case that looks like an edge case no real user would ever hit. How do you decide whether to fix the code or fix the test?
drills.a: Determine whether the stated invariant is genuinely required for correctness in production (if so, fix the code even if the input is rare) or whether the invariant itself was mis-stated/too strong for the actual contract (if so, relax or correct the property). Dismissing the failure without making this determination either ships a latent bug or leaves a wrong test in the suite.

drills.q: Explain why using a Mock (with assert_called_once()) where a Stub would have sufficed can cause a test to fail for an unrelated, harmless reason.
drills.a: If the mock's call count is asserted unnecessarily, an unrelated refactor that adds a harmless second no-op call (e.g., a caching layer checking then calling through) breaks the test even though the actual behavior under test -- correct use of the returned data -- is completely unaffected. A stub used purely to supply data, with the assertion placed on what the unit under test does with that data, wouldn't have this false-positive failure mode.
